passage: Rashmi leaned into the microphone. "Yash, I learned this in my first year as a manager, at twenty-five. The sales team got a new perk: a travel allowance and a quarterly dinner. My support team didn't. Everyone's salary was fair, above the market rate in fact. But within a month my team was sulking. People stopped staying late. One of them said, 'We fix their mistakes, and they get dinners.' I realised it wasn't about money. It was about feeling left behind next to the people one desk away. So I went to management and got the criteria written down: why sales got travel money, which was for actual travel, and what would earn my team the same kind of recognition. I explained it straight, in a team meeting. It didn't fix everything. But the sulking eased once people could see the rules."

qa.q: What new perk did the sales team get?
qa.a: A travel allowance and a quarterly dinner.

qa.q: What did Rashmi realise was really behind the sulking?
qa.a: It wasn't about money; the team felt left out next to people one desk away who got perks.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do, and why did it ease the resentment?
qa.a: Rashmi got the criteria written down and explained them plainly in a team meeting, so people could see the rules instead of guessing at unfairness.

qa.q: How might the sales team have seen the support team's sulking?
qa.a: The sales team may have been puzzled, seeing the travel allowance as a practical need rather than a reward over others.

grounding: A young manager notices resentment in a fairly paid team when another team gets perks, and eases it with transparent criteria and an honest explanation.

passage: I'm Parul, and I teach in the department Vasudha heads. Last term the school gave new laptops to the senior teachers only. We were all paid on the same scale and nobody was underpaid, but the junior staff went quiet in a way I hadn't seen before. They stopped volunteering for events. Someone left a note on the staffroom board: "Seniors: laptops. Juniors: chalk." Vasudha noticed. I saw her read the note twice and leave it up. At the next meeting she laid out exactly how the laptops had been allotted, by years of service, and admitted the rule had never been explained. Then she got the management to publish when the juniors would get theirs. I can't say what she felt, but her voice was steady. The note came down on its own a week later.

qa.q: What did the note on the staffroom board say?
qa.a: "Seniors: laptops. Juniors: chalk."

qa.q: What does Vasudha reading the note twice and leaving it up suggest?
qa.a: She seemed to take the junior staff's resentment seriously rather than wanting to hide it.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do at the next meeting, and why did it help?
qa.a: She explained how laptops were allotted by years of service, admitted it hadn't been explained, and got a published date for juniors, making the criteria transparent.

qa.q: How might the junior staff feel once the date for their laptops was published?
qa.a: They may feel less left behind, since the rule was now clear and they could see when their turn would come.

grounding: A colleague watches a head of department notice resentment among fairly paid junior staff over a perk and reduce it with clear criteria and an honest explanation.

passage: Week one. Head office announced a festive bonus for the loans team only. Salma, twenty-six and managing the accounts team next door, saw Elizabeth's face harden as she read the email. By Friday the accounts team had stopped chatting with loans at lunch. Week three. The resentment had grown. Elizabeth snapped at a loans officer over a small form. Salma called the regional manager and asked plainly, "What were the criteria?" The answer: the bonus was tied to a loan target accounts had no part in, and accounts had received a pay revision in April that nobody remembered. Week five. Salma put both facts on one slide and explained them at a team meeting, along with the targets that could earn accounts a bonus next year. Elizabeth asked two questions, nodded, and on Friday ate lunch with loans again.

qa.q: Which team got the festive bonus?
qa.a: The loans team.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's hardened face suggest about how she felt reading the email?
qa.a: She felt left out and resentful that the loans team got a bonus while her team did not.

qa.q: What did Salma do in week five, and why did it work?
qa.a: Salma put the bonus criteria and the April pay revision on one slide and explained what could earn accounts a bonus, so the team saw the reasons and a path forward.

qa.q: How might the loans officer have felt when Elizabeth snapped over a small form?
qa.a: The loans officer may have been confused and hurt, not knowing the snap came from resentment about the bonus.

grounding: A young manager notices resentment when another team gets a bonus despite fair pay, and eases it over weeks with transparent criteria and an honest explanation.

passage: Devika, sit. You're new at managing, so let me tell you about my first year on the floor at the garment unit. I was twenty-four. That summer the company put new standing fans and padded stools in the cutting section. Stitching got nothing. Pay was the same for both, fair pay, above the other units in the area. But within two weeks the stitching women stopped talking to the cutting men at tea. Someone scratched "cutting = kings" on the stitching room door. I noticed and, at first, I thought, they're being childish. Then I asked why the fans went to cutting. Nobody had told us: the cutting room had been measured as the hottest. So I got the measurements, showed them to both sections, and got a date in writing for stitching's fans. Listen to an old man, beta. Your team can swallow a lot. What they can't swallow is not knowing why. - Wasim

qa.q: What did the company put in the cutting section that summer?
qa.a: It put new standing fans and padded stools in the cutting section.

qa.q: What did Wasim first think when he noticed the resentment, and how did that change?
qa.a: At first he thought the stitching workers were being childish, but after asking why the fans went to cutting he realised nobody had explained the reason.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how Wasim handled it?
qa.a: Getting the heat measurements, showing them to both sections and securing a written date for stitching's fans made the rule visible and fair.

qa.q: How did the stitching workers experience the new fans in cutting?
qa.a: They felt left behind and treated as less important, even with fair pay, which showed in the silence at tea and the words scratched on the door.

grounding: A young manager notices resentment in one section when another gets perks despite fair pay, and eases it with clear criteria and an honest explanation.

passage: The quarterly review was on Monday, and Himani, twenty-six and managing the day shift at the call centre, had one weekend to deal with the mood on her floor. Since the company started a free cab for the night shift, her day team had gone cold. Pallavi, usually the first to help new joiners, now sat with her headphones on at lunch. On Friday Himani heard her mutter, "Night shift gets cars, we get nothing." Everyone was on the same pay scale. Then the rain started and half her team was stuck at home, so there was no chance of a meeting. Himani asked HR for the cab rule in writing: it was for safety after midnight. She put it in one clear message to the team, with the pay scale beside it, and added the shift allowance day staff could apply for. On Monday Pallavi took her headphones off at lunch.

qa.q: What did the company start for the night shift?
qa.a: It started a free cab for the night shift.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's muttered comment suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels left out and resentful, as if the day shift is valued less, even though pay is the same.

qa.q: What did Himani do well despite the rain keeping her team at home?
qa.a: She got the cab rule in writing and sent one clear message explaining the safety reason, the equal pay scale and an allowance day staff could apply for.

qa.q: How might the night shift have seen the day team's coldness?
qa.a: The night shift might have been confused or hurt by it, since the cab was for their safety after midnight, not a reward.

grounding: A young manager notices resentment when one shift gets a perk despite fair pay, and reduces it with transparent criteria and an honest explanation.

passage: Manoj, twenty-six, had been team lead at the Pune office for six months when he noticed the change. The sales team had got new laptops and a monthly team dinner, thanks to a client bonus. The support team, where Wasim worked, got nothing. Everyone's pay was fair and within the same bands, Manoj knew. But in the canteen, the support staff sat apart, and Wasim muttered, "Some of us are only here to fix their mess." Manoj heard it. He felt a knot of worry. He didn't think Wasim was wrong to feel that way. So at the next team meeting he laid it all out: what the client bonus was, how it was decided, and that support would get a similar reward if their ticket goals were met. He wrote the criteria on the whiteboard. Wasim crossed his arms, but he stayed and asked questions.

qa.q: What did the sales team get thanks to the client bonus?
qa.a: They got new laptops and a monthly team dinner.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when he heard Wasim's comment?
qa.a: Manoj felt a knot of worry, understanding why the support team might feel left out.

qa.q: Why did writing the criteria on the whiteboard help?
qa.a: Clear, visible rules for rewards made the process feel fair, reducing the sense that support was being left behind.

qa.q: How might Wasim see the situation after the meeting?
qa.a: Wasim is still wary, arms crossed, but he stays and asks questions, suggesting he is starting to trust the explanation.

grounding: A manager notices resentment when one team gets perks and another doesn't, even with fair pay, and uses transparent criteria and honest explanation.

passage:
"Aditi, got a minute?" Akash asked, leaning on her desk.
"Sure." She didn't look up.
"You've been quiet since the night-shift allowance was announced."
"Well, the night team gets extra, and we get nothing. Same work."
"Same tasks, yes. But they work eleven to seven."
"I know. It's just... we hear about it every day. Like they're special."
"Do you think your pay is unfair?"
Aditi paused. "No. It's fine. It just feels like we're forgotten."
Akash nodded. "That's fair to feel. I should've explained how the allowance works, and that anyone can apply for night shifts."
"Anyone?"
"Anyone. I'll put the policy on the team board today."
Aditi finally looked up. "That would help. Honestly, I didn't even know we could apply."

qa.q: What hours does the night team work?
qa.a: They work eleven to seven.

qa.q: What was Akash thinking when he came to Aditi's desk?
qa.a: Akash felt concerned, having noticed Aditi's quiet resentment since the allowance was announced.

qa.q: What did Akash do that reduced Aditi's resentment?
qa.a: Akash listened, acknowledged her feelings, and promised to share the allowance policy openly, making the criteria clear.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel about the night-shift allowance?
qa.a: Aditi felt forgotten and resentful, even though she agreed her own pay was fair.

grounding: A manager notices resentment when one shift gets an allowance and another doesn't, and uses honest explanation and clear criteria to ease it.

passage: I still think about my first year as a warehouse supervisor in Nashik. I was twenty-five, a young man with twelve people under me. When the morning shift got new jackets and hot lunch because they handled the refrigerated section, the evening shift turned cold on me. Deepak, the evening loader, a hard worker, stopped joking. He said once, not quite to me, "Some people are more valuable, I guess." Their pay was the same as the morning shift's, and fair. I knew that. But I hadn't explained why the jackets and lunches went to one group. So I called both shifts together, showed them the cold-room rules, and said evening staff could rotate into the cold room if they wanted. Deepak was the first to sign up. I'm Tejas. That was when I learnt that fair isn't enough; it has to look fair too.

qa.q: How many people did Tejas supervise?
qa.a: Tejas had twelve people under him.

qa.q: What was Tejas thinking when Deepak stopped joking?
qa.a: Tejas felt uneasy and responsible, realising the evening shift felt undervalued because nothing had been explained.

qa.q: Which change worked, and why?
qa.a: Explaining the cold-room rules and letting evening staff rotate in made the perks' criteria clear and open, easing the resentment.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt when he signed up first?
qa.a: Deepak probably felt included and respected again, seeing that the perks weren't about some people being more valuable.

grounding: A young supervisor looks back on noticing resentment when one shift got perks, and using honest explanation and open criteria to reduce it.

passage:
Team note, week 12, by Lalit (sales manager)
After the tech team got new laptops and a team lunch, I noticed changes on the sales side. Kamal stopped joining the morning huddle. Two others muttered about "favourites." Nobody on sales was paid less; their laptops simply weren't due yet.
I didn't want to guess, so I asked Kamal privately. "It feels like we don't count," Kamal said.
On Monday I shared the replacement schedule with the whole team: which laptops were due when, and why. I also said the lunch was for the tech release, and that sales would get one after the quarter.
Kamal came back to the huddle on Wednesday. Asked questions, too.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when the tech team got perks?
qa.a: Kamal felt left out and undervalued, as if the sales team didn't count.

grounding: Shows a manager noticing resentment when one team gets perks, and easing it with clear criteria and an honest explanation.

passage: Kamal had managed the dairy cooperative in Anand for a year when the grumbling started. At Diwali the milk-collection staff had got a bonus for the record monsoon season; the plant workers had not. Everyone was paid fairly by the book, but Kamal noticed the plant workers eating separately and the jokes turning sharp. Shankar, who had run the chilling plant for twenty years, stopped saying good morning. Kamal didn't wait for things to boil over. He called a meeting under the neem tree and put the bonus criteria on a chart: litres collected, new farmers signed. 'You're right that it only rewarded one kind of work,' he said. 'That's my mistake.' He proposed a new rule for next year, with a plant target too, and asked Shankar to help set it. Shankar folded his arms, then nodded slowly.

passage: Fatima had been promoted to team manager at the Toronto software firm in January. By March she noticed something odd: the office-based designers had gone quiet in meetings, and Astrid, usually the first to joke, answered in single words. It took Fatima a week to find the reason. The remote engineers had been given a home-office allowance; the designers, who came in every day, got nothing extra. No one was underpaid. But to the designers it looked as if one group was valued more. Fatima went to Astrid first. 'I think the allowance feels unfair to your team. Am I right?' Astrid exhaled. 'Yes. Nobody explained it.' That afternoon Fatima wrote to the whole team, laying out why the allowance existed, and proposed a matching commuting benefit to HR.

passage: On the general ward of the Chennai hospital, the nurses' station had grown cold. Anjali, the young nurse in charge, noticed it first in small things: nobody shared snacks with the ICU team any more, and Gautam, the most cheerful nurse on nights, muttered 'VIPs' whenever an ICU nurse walked past. She asked him about it over tea at 3 am. 'The ICU got the new training trip to Bengaluru and new uniforms,' Gautam said. 'We work just as hard.' Anjali knew the pay scales were identical. But she also knew nobody had explained how the trip was chosen. The next morning she asked the nursing superintendent for the criteria, posted them on the notice board and pushed for the next training slot to go to the ward. By the end of the month the snacks were being shared again.

qa.q: What did the ICU get?
qa.a: The new training trip to Bengaluru and new uniforms.

qa.q: What did Anjali feel as she noticed the cold nurses' station?

qa.q: Why did posting the criteria help?
qa.a: It made clear how the perks were chosen, so the ward felt less left behind and could see a fair path to the next slot.

passage:
Subject: Mood in support after the field-team allowance
Hi Gurleen,
Since the field sales team got the new travel allowance and laptops last month, the mood in my support team has soured. Nobody's pay changed; our salaries were checked against the market in April and are fair. But at lunch I hear "we're the second-class team" and "they're the favourites". Two people have stopped joining the Friday call. I don't think it's greed. I think they can't see why one group got something and they didn't.
My plan: at Thursday's team meeting I'll explain exactly what the allowance covers (fuel and client travel) and why support doesn't qualify, and share the written criteria for all perks. I'd also like us to ask whether support needs anything specific, like better headsets.
Could you join, so it isn't just my opinion?
Amandeep

qa.q: What did the field sales team get last month?
qa.a: The new travel allowance and laptops.

qa.q: What does Amandeep think is behind the team's resentment?
qa.a: Amandeep feels concerned but understanding, believing it is not greed but hurt at not seeing why one group got something and they didn't.

qa.q: Why is Amandeep's plan likely to help?
qa.a: Explaining what the allowance covers, sharing written criteria and asking what support needs makes fairness visible, so people feel less left behind.

qa.q: How do the support team members seem to see the allowance?

grounding: A manager notices resentment when one team gets perks although everyone is paid fairly, and plans clear criteria and an honest explanation.
